tier_reason: Chapter02/01_substring_sort.C, 03_substring_sort.C and 04_substring_sort.C (shared setup 00_substring_sort_prep.C, compare() in the matching _a.C files) are public and differ only in the compare() loop (bounded unsigned, unbounded unsigned, unbounded int), with -g -O3 build comments, but the compiler is only '$CXX, usually GCC or CLANG' (Chapter02/ReadMe.md), no CPU is named and no results exist in the repo; the 98/210/74 ms figures are the book's own (first-party), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Book-reported (relayed via the seed lead; no numbers anywhere in the repository): the sort takes 98 ms with the bounded unsigned compare, 210 ms with the unsigned compare without the bound check, and 74 ms with the signed int index compare, so the signed version is about 1.3x faster than the bounded unsigned one and about 2.8x faster than the unbounded unsigned one (both derived from the relayed book figures).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: $CXX, unspecified (Chapter02/ReadMe.md: 'usually GCC or CLANG'), with -g -O3 -I. --std=c++17 per the build comment in each Chapter02 0N_substring_sort.C; no LTO, so compare() in its own translation unit is not inlined
corrections.workload: Chapter02 01/03/04_substring_sort.C with the shared setup 00_substring_sort_prep.C (option C): std::sort of 2^14 pointers to random offsets in a 2^18-byte NUL-terminated string that is all 'a' except 256 randomly placed random letters (about one per 1024 chars), using a lambda that counts comparisons and calls compare() defined in a separate translation unit; wall time of the sort only, by std::chrono::system_clock, single run.
corrections.caveats: The timing numbers are the book's own (quoted in the seed lead); the repository carries the benchmark program but no results file, so the numbers do not appear on the benchmark_url page and the ratios could not be checked against it. Compiler is only 'GCC or Clang'. Baseline is a hand-written byte loop, not std::memcmp or std::strcmp, which would probably beat all three variants and was not tried. It is odd that the unbounded unsigned loop (210 ms) is slower than the bounded one (98 ms); the explanation is compiler-specific code generation, so another compiler or version may show a different ordering. Single timed run with a deterministic minstd_rand seed; the data are almost constant, so many comparisons run to the end of a long equal prefix. [verifier] By reading the source (not compiled or run here): the bounded variant's limit is L, the whole 2^18-byte string length, not the remaining length; the buffer ends in a single NUL and compare() returns early when s1 == s2, so every call ends on a mismatch before the limit, all three variants return the same result, and the bound check is pure per-byte overhead. 01 against 04 changes two things (drops the bound and its parameter, and switches to a signed index); 03 against 04 isolates the signedness. A likely mechanism, not confirmed by disassembly here: signed overflow is undefined, so the compiler may widen the int index to a 64-bit pointer offset, while an unbounded unsigned int index must wrap modulo 2^32 and needs per-step zero-extension; the bound i1 < l lets the compiler prove no wrap, which would explain why the bounded unsigned loop beats the unbounded one. Chapter02 also carries Google Benchmark microbenchmarks of the same three compare functions (10a_compare_mbm.C, and 11_compare_mbm.C with compare() in separate files 11_compare_mbm_a/b/c.C, plus the 12_compare_mbm_* variants) on a 2^20-byte all-'a' buffer, but no results for them either. The build comments in 03_substring_sort.C and 04_substring_sort.C both name the output binary 01_substring_sort (copy-paste), so building as written overwrites the 01 binary. Timing uses system_clock rather than steady_clock, and the timed lambda also increments a comparison counter (same in all variants).
